claim: An agent-controlled context compression architecture (Focus), where the agent itself decides when to consolidate and prune its own history via start_focus/complete_focus tool calls, reduced total token consumption by 22.7% (14,920,555 to 11,526,418 tokens) across 5 hard SWE-bench Lite instances while maintaining identical task-success accuracy (3/5 = 60%) to an uncompressed baseline using Claude Haiku 4.5.
stance_target: agent-autonomous (not externally-imposed) context compression can cut cost without sacrificing task quality, a measured benchmark for the cost-optimization pillar
scope_conditions: N=5 context-intensive SWE-bench Lite instances, Claude Haiku 4.5, two-tool scaffold (persistent bash + string-replace editor), published Jan 2026
quoted_support: Focus achieves 22.7% token reduction (14.9M →11.5M tokens) while maintaining identical accuracy (3/5 = 60% for both agents).

claim: Passive/infrequent compression prompting caused measurable accuracy degradation (60% vs 80% baseline in earlier experiments) whereas aggressive prompting that mandates compression every 10-15 tool calls, reinforced by system-injected reminders, eliminated the accuracy tradeoff entirely while still delivering the token savings -- implying that compression frequency/timing, not merely whether to compress, is the critical design variable.
stance_target: context compression inherently trades off against task accuracy
quoted_support: The key insight: when and how often to compress matters more than whether to compress. Frequent small compressions (every 10-15 calls) preserve recent context while discarding stale exploration logs, whereas infrequent large compressions risk losing critical implementation details.

claim: Current LLMs do not naturally optimize for context/token efficiency on their own; achieving significant compression gains (22.7% vs. only 6% with passive prompting) required explicit, directive scaffolding instructing the model to compress on a fixed cadence, indicating context-efficient behavior must be engineered into the harness rather than assumed as an emergent model capability.
stance_target: architecture/scaffolding, not raw model capability, determines whether cost-optimization goals are achieved in agentic loops
quoted_support: Current models appear to lack intrinsic cost-awareness—they do not naturally optimize for token efficiency... This indicates that current LLMs do not naturally optimize for context efficiency—they require scaffolding that makes compression a first-class part of the workflow.

claim: Context compression benefit is task-dependent: exploration-heavy tasks (codebase navigation, e.g., matplotlib-26020 and sympy-21171) showed 50-57% token savings, while one iterative-refinement task (pylint-7080) showed a 110% token INCREASE because compressions discarded context that later had to be re-derived, exceeding the compression benefit.
stance_target: aggressive context compression is universally beneficial for all agentic task types
scope_conditions: 5 SWE-bench Lite instances with Claude Haiku 4.5
quoted_support: This case shows that compression is not universally beneficial: tasks requiring iterative refinement may suffer from aggressive context pruning... On pylint-7080, Focus used 110% more tokens than Baseline (4.3M vs. 2.1M), yet both agents passed the test suite.
